item.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI (169 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://architectlabs.com/blog/frostbite, See on Hacker News

Abstract

In our previous post, Redwood, we showed that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?”

Today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core.

Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts.

Introduction to interaction nets

Mainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly.

Interaction nets1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because each node has exactly one principal port, no two of these active pairs ever overlap, so they can be rewritten in any order, or all at once, and the result is always the same. Interaction nets are also linear: every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state for the hardware to guard. Languages such as Vine2compile ordinary-looking programs directly to interaction nets. For an excellent introduction to interaction nets and why they suit hardware, we highly recommend Tendrils' “On Interaction Nets.” 3

Fig. 1 shows the difference on a small search problem, placing five queens on a five-by-five board. The sequential program visits one candidate at a time. The interaction net exposes all of its independent work: on average, about twelve interactions are ready to run at every step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get this parallelism; the dependencies were simply never thrown away.

In theory, this should have two large advantages. The first is multithreading for free: rather than varying levels of coarse and fine-grained parallelism, parallelism comes straight from the program. No threads, locks, or race conditions, and none of the out-of-order machinery a conventional core uses to dig it back out. The second is that, since every value has one owner and every step is local, data can live in small local memories next to where it is used. That removes much of the area and power a conventional chip spends on large caching subsystems, and much of the system-level complexity of keeping those caches coherent.

Process

Frostbite was designed with zero architectural priors. We followed the process below, riding multiple agent swarms along the way.

Architecture exploration and selection

To begin architectural exploration, we had to establish the set of workloads Frostbite should do exceedingly well in. We decided to look at different ways a program could expose its work: many independent pieces at once, rounds of parallel work, long sequential chains, data-dependent branches, and recursion. Under each category, we created a search set and a held-out eval set to evaluate the final Frostbite on, ensuring the design generalized to programs it was never tuned on. The kernels for FFT, radixsort, and LU follow the implementation in the SPLASH-2 benchmark, although 64 times smaller, because at regular sizes they are not suitable for exploratory work.

Later, we added five more practical workloads to the held-out set: a Kalman filter, PCA, finite element analysis, an LU solve, and LZ4 decompression.

Agents synthesized research papers and existing benchmarks, and built Python models to trade off high-level architectural ideas against each other, before narrowing to a single architectural concept. The output of this exploration was a 141-page PDF covering the proposed programming model, the runtime, and the high-level blocks of the chip. This was nowhere near the final architecture, but rather a starting point where all the prior findings, high-level requirements, constraints, experiments, and runtime traits were described. Once the first architectural iteration completed (first RTL generation), this was deleted, since many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible.

Formal contracts and system modeling

Once the architecture candidate was selected, our system moved on to building the full software model of the chip. Building software models is essential when exploring an architectural space, as they allow fast iteration between the workloads, the ISA, and the abstracted view of the hardware. Whether we build a CPU, GPU, NPU, or networking switch, mastering this iteration loop allows the fastest exploration of the design space within a finite time. To do this repeatedly, we designed a new in-house specification language, ASL, and wrote Frostbite's system model “Arcmodel” in it. ASL supports machine-checkable translations and refinements between RTL, system models, UVM, SVA, and more, all against a formally backed specification. Its power and performance estimates are accurate to within 1–5%, it runs roughly 200x faster than RTL simulation, and it is formally verifiable through “contracts.”

In every silicon program to date, human architects have written many English PDFs before handing off to an implementation team and a verification team. However, natural language cannot capture every detail an implementation needs precisely and unambiguously, and it cannot guarantee that every agent hallucination is caught while the ASIC is being designed and verified. Natural language was never built for this, and in a world where AI writes the specification, we opt for a formal, machine-checkable specification language instead.

ASL can formally describe both high-level, protocol-like behavior, such as out-of-order handling, CSR programming, memory ordering, and coherency, and low-level details, such as pipelines, arbitration mechanisms, and compute transfer functions. This lets the model leave the specification open-ended where that is useful and constrain it exactly where a precise behavior is required. ASL also translates natively to Lean,4 which we use for all theorem proving when checking AI outputs across RTL, UVM, C, SVA, and more. We will discuss ASL in more detail in a future post.

Throughout the entire development of Frostbite, our AI iterates on the Frostbite ISA, Arcmodel, Design, and Verification tightly together, maintaining the ASL Contract as the source of truth. We've found that having a single, provable source of truth prevents a large class of bugs, silly mistakes, and reward-hacking instances when deploying large agent swarms. Ultimately, this common language allows the models to work across the stack nimbly, reflecting the changes propagated from the workload down to the final hardware. By the end, our Frostbite ASL lowered down to 800k+ lines of Lean.

RTL and alignment

Because ASL is a formally backed specification, designing and verifying the RTL derived from it is the fastest part of the entire Frostbite process. Arcmodel, however, is not physically aware, so its power and performance estimates at first diverge from the true numbers of the timing-converged, synthesis-clean RTL, in the worst case by almost 250%.

Before continuing the ASL autoresearch, one of our systems recalibrates Arcmodel against the RTL. This is a fully autonomous pipeline. It first identifies the power hotspots in the RTL and traces them down to key counters in the formal specification, such as SRAM reads and writes, operation counts, flits sent and received, credit returns, and frame misses. The model may then write any scalar Python function over those counters to predict power, and it repeats this process until the RTL and Arcmodel agree to within 5%.

We find this style of non-gradient learning extremely powerful. Once this first physical alignment has been applied, later iterations are much faster. These are, of course, still pre-silicon power numbers, and over multiple tapeout loops, ASL models can be correlated to true post-silicon, production power numbers.

By aligning the Arcmodel and RTL so closely, the continued swarms were able to explore and exploit much faster. The full Arcmodel chip simulations are much faster than the RTL (660x faster), which led to many cross-stack optimizations. For instance, our AI systems discovered very fine-grained clock gating tricks, and adjusted the software runtime accordingly to accommodate them in a matter of hours. Such a cross-stack optimization is near-impossible to execute on in a traditional ASIC flow.

Contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power, iterated together

Once Arcmodel and the RTL agreed, the original Python models and the architecture PDF were deleted, and the ASL contracts became the only specification of the chip. From then on, contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power moved forward together. Swarms of agents proposed architecture revisions in parallel worktrees; each change was checked against the contracts, modeled in Arcmodel, implemented in RTL, and measured for power, and then either kept or dropped. Across four searches and a final round of ablations, the swarm tried 58 ideas and kept 37 of them, from clock gates on a running tile to smaller L3 tables and one shared expander.

Architectural novelty

The architecture in full detail would warrant its own post. Instead, we choose to focus here on the features that we considered either novel or creative and highlight the capability of our systems to push the frontiers of hardware design.

Programs for Frostbite are written in Vine,2 which is a fully fledged programming language with syntax similar to Rust. A Vine program is compiled to Ivy, an intermediate representation (IR) that encodes the interaction net structure. The optimizer also tries to apply as many of the graph reduction rules as it can, so the final Ivy net, as it is called, has a (mostly) fixed shape, composed of three primitives: data, computation nodes, and control nodes. However, the runtime of this net is still very dynamic, because unlike the typical computation graph, where the parallelism is encoded in the structure and pipelined over time, the parallelism has to be derived at runtime from the state and pipelined spatially. The initial naïve implementations were slow, so our agents had to get creative.

The generated ISA follows from this set of constraints. A lot of it is expected: wide bundles, hardware loop counters, and streams. We found the dynamic features more interesting, particularly operations to take, peek, and copy values from other parts of the net that would be running in parallel. The tiles then come alive, communicating across space.

Emergent property: stealing work

Because the parallelism is spread over space, there is no central scheduler. Instead, we saw the agents design these elegant rules for propagating the work. A tile follows three rules: it runs its own work first, meaning work in its input ports. If those are empty, it takes work from a neighboring tile that has work to spare. If no such tile is found, it can just go inactive and save power.

The agents demonstrated remarkable sophistication in how they implemented this. Below, we have the hardware for a single Frostbite tile:

A lot of them should be familiar. We are interested in the RUNTIME domain that is responsible for the work-stealing behavior described above.

The compiler breaks code into short sections that run uninterrupted once their inputs are ready. These are run in the engine and are mostly organized like traditional computation through the front end. Whenever a loop or branch splits into parallel pieces whose sizes aren't known ahead of time, the running section parks whatever comes after into a small record in local memory, the frame manager. It then drops the new tasks onto a hardware queue called the work queue and picks up the newest one itself. Idle neighbors are then free to pull the remaining tasks over the network. As tasks finish anywhere on the chip in any order, their return packets tick down the parked record's counter and automatically wake the next section the instant the last piece arrives.

This is what it looks like in hardware:

We can think of each “task” as the current board, one level down, with one more queen. Tile 0 has to queue three tasks for all the possible queen configurations before it can finish the present board state. It's free, so it takes the newest task (from itself) and runs it. Meanwhile, its neighbors have gotten the other ones, except for Tile 5, which goes back to sleep.

This behavior was never specified by any human. We can directly trace it back to necessity on specific regressions and hill-climbing performance metrics.

Results

We synthesized Frostbite on a 7 nm process, reaching 800 MHz timing at synthesis and 500 MHz in the final GDS. Each Frostbite quad (a two-by-two grid of tiles) paired with four L3 nodes is 0.792 mm². We benchmark one Quad+L3 cluster against a single core of a modern superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU, which we refer to as TCPU (“Traditional CPU”). This TCPU is 0.895 mm² at the same process.†

We benchmarked on a wide set of workloads, from dense, parallel kernels such as gemm and conv2d, to irregular, branching programs such as JSON parsing, Huffman coding, k-d trees, and recursive Fibonacci. A search set of workloads drove all architectural optimization, ISA design, RTL, and verification, and the chip was evaluated on both the 10 search-set workloads and the 15 held out, including the five practical workloads added later (Fig. 3).

For a fair comparison, we chose to first measure “single-core” performance by benchmarking one Frostbite quad against the TCPU, since they have similar area. Across all the workloads, we average an 8.77x performance-per-area, and across all 25 workloads, search set and held out together, Frostbite reaches a geometric mean of 4.59x the TCPU's performance-per-watt: 6.02x on the 10 search-set workloads, and 3.83x on the 15 held-out workloads it was never tuned on. As expected, the architecture does most strongly on highly parallelizable tasks, but it also outperforms the TCPU on branching, dynamic code.

The energy breakdown shows where the savings come from. Leaving out clock distribution (49% of TCPU energy, 41% of a Frostbite quad's), the TCPU spends 57% of its energy on memory and 27% on fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions. Frostbite cuts memory to 38% and fetch, decode, and issue to just 6%. In exchange, it spends 26% on its on-chip network and scheduler, the cost of sharing work and moving messages between tiles. What's more exciting, however, is that as we scale the chip to a four-by-four array (four quads), the power distribution is relatively the same. In a general-purpose multi-core CPU arrangement, scaling the number of cores requires adding heavy coherency mechanisms and large caches, whereas when running interaction nets, the same data locality rules always apply, and more cores do not increase system complexity. This is illustrated below. In the coming months, we'll be benchmarking Frostbite mesh-like configurations against multi-core “TCPU” arrangements with large caches and larger, wider, out-of-order CPUs, over a larger set of industry benchmarks such as SPEC and PARSEC.

What comes next

While interaction nets have been around for more than 35 years, their production value has never been fully clear. Historically, there has always been a risk of exploring out-of-distribution architectures, for the time, investment, and labor required to come to conviction. We believe AI fundamentally changes these economics. In the search for higher performance and lower power, extreme co-design of workloads, ISA, and hardware will continue to be demanded. With large agent swarms, sophisticated search-space techniques, precise guardrails, formal verification, and faster EDA tools, AI systems will be able to discover and build novel accelerators at a quality that exceeds human cognition. While there is much more to do, we feel it is the right time to share with the world what the future of autonomous chip design could look like. We plan to continue scaling development on Frostbite, including but not limited to:

  • Deliver a software playground for anybody to run a program on Frostbite, hosted on FPGAs.
  • Build a preliminary operating system capable of managing hardware resources, multiple programs, virtualization, and more.
  • Scale swarms to bring Frostbite to higher performance-per-watt, and benchmark it on a much larger set of workloads against a broader set of CPUs.
  • Release the RTL and ISA for Frostbite.

We are having a lot of fun!

Notes

†For legal reasons, we cannot disclose the exact CPU.

References

  1. 1.Lafont, Y. (1990). “Interaction Nets.” Proceedings of the 17th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL ’90), 95–108. doi:10.1145/96709.96718
  2. 2.The Vine programming language. vine.dev
  3. 3.Tendrils (2026). “On Interaction Nets.” tendrils.co/blog/2026-04-26/on-inets
  4. 4.de Moura, L., and Ullrich, S. (2021). “The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language.” Automated Deduction – CADE 28, LNCS 12699, 625–635. doi:10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37

item.title: Carnival Cruises emits ten times more sulphur oxide than all of Europe's cars (2019) (170 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ecohustler.com/article/one-corporation-to-pollute-them-all/, See on Hacker News

In April, Ecohustler disrupted Carnival Cruise's AGM calling on the shareholders to reduce their company's pollution using straight forward and affordable methods - like burning cleaner fuel. Since then, a new report outlines the corporation's impact on the coastline of Europe. These vast floating cities are burning dirty bunker fuel and creating shocking levels of air pollution wherever they go. Shipping has been an unregulated industry for too long and action is urgently required.

Carnival Corporation, the world’s largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly 10 times more sulphur oxide (SOx) around European coasts than did all 260 million European cars in 2017, a new analysis by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals.

Royal Caribbean Cruises, the world’s second largest, is second, yet four times worse than the European car fleet. SOx emissions form sulphate (SO4) aerosols that increase human health risks and contribute to acidification in terrestrial and aquatic environments.

SUPPORTED BY HEROES LIKE YOU

Support independent eco journalism that drives real change.

JOIN US →

In absolute terms, Spain, Italy and Greece, closely followed by France and Norway, are the European countries most exposed to SOx air pollution from cruise vessels while Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca and Venice are the most impacted European port cities, followed by Civitavecchia (Rome) and Southampton.

All photos by Greg English ©

These countries are so exposed because they are major tourist destinations, but also because they have less stringent marine sulphur fuel standards which allows cruise ships to burn the dirtiest most sulphurous fuel all along their coastlines.

Faig Abbasov, shipping policy manager at T&E, said: “Luxury cruise ships are floating cities powered by some of the dirtiest fuel possible. Cities are rightly banning dirty diesel cars but they’re giving a free pass to cruise companies that spew out toxic fumes that do immeasurable harm both to those on board and on nearby shores. This is unacceptable.“

NOX emissions from cruise ships in Europe also heavily impact some cities, equivalent to about 15% of the nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted by Europe’s passenger car fleet in a year, the report finds. In Marseille, for example, 57 cruise ships emitted in 2017 almost as much NOx as one-quarter of the city’s 340,000 passenger cars. Along the coasts of countries such as Norway, Denmark, Greece, Croatia and Malta a handful of cruise ships are also responsible for more NOx than the majority of their domestic car fleet.

Europe should implement a zero-emission port standard as soon as possible, this could then be extended to other ship types. The report also recommends extending emission control areas (ECAs), currently in place only in the North and Baltic Seas and English Channel, to the rest of the European seas. Furthermore, the report recommends regulating NOx emissions from existing ships, which are currently exempt from NOx standards applying in emission control areas.

Faig Abbasov concluded “There are enough mature technologies to clean up cruise ships. Shore-side electricity can help cut in-port emissions, batteries are a solution for shorter distances and hydrogen technology can power even the biggest cruise ships. The cruise sector are apparently not willing to make the shift voluntarily, so we need governments to step in and mandate zero emission standards.”

item.title: "I can tell you wrote this yourself" (240 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://em-online.bearblog.dev/i-can-tell-you-wrote-this-yourself/, See on Hacker News

19 Nov, 2026

Those were some of the first words my honours project supervisor said to me last week when we met to discuss a progress report I had written to mark the midway point of the project.

It's a roughly 10-page report on the control of flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles - which is probably very boring unless you're particularly interested in that. I accidentally set the due date for the report a week early in my calendar, so after spending 48 hours stressed and pumping out 5,000 words, citing references and adding diagrams1, I was pleasantly relieved to find I'd tricked myself into being quite productive. I had a lot of time to get my supervisor to review the report and action his feedback.

When he told me he could tell I wrote it myself, I wasn't sure how to take it. A compliment? An insult? Then he followed it up with:

"I've been sent a lot of reports written by AI."

At first this shocked me. Our reports are limited to 10 pages - so the appendices are getting a big workout around here - how hard is it to right 10 pages yourself?

But then I thought about what the last year of my engineering degree has been like.

Assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which quickly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day.

The reason why we've been pushed to use it?

Apparently it's the way the industry is going. Apparently actually knowing things doesn't matter nearly so much as knowing how to prompt a machine to do the thing. Apparently the future of engineering - at least in my field - is to become a glorified babysitter. The AI isn't going anywhere, they say, so it's best we learn how to manage it well.

But sitting in a room telling an AI "ignore the approaching deadline, we still have 8 hours, keep working" isn't exactly filling me with enthusiasm for the rest of my career.

It's soul crushing, and I don't want to outsource so much of my thinking to it.

In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy, I don't want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline, I can't help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea.

It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all?

Because I worry that it starts with using it for an assignment when you're encouraged to, but then it turns into relying on it to write a 10-page report on a project you should know back-to-front. A project that you'll have to present and defend in person when it finishes. And then you're asking it for advice, using it to summarise books, turning to it for anything you would normally look up or ask a friend.

The internet is riddled with AI content that is making it increasingly more difficult to tell fact from fiction. In a world where everything is so polarised and deliberately provoking, the ability to identify bias or motivation in the content we consume has perhaps never been more important. Being able to think for ourselves has perhaps never been more important.

As the tech world continues to offer us increasingly more opportunities to automate things, I'm practically begging you to please not automate your thinking.

Read the books. Write the papers. Search for answers instead of asking AI. Ask a friend. Ask your mum about the mystery illness you're convinced you're developing and then take her advice and try drinking a glass of water.

Think about what the creators of the content you consume want you to think2. Treat the things you consume like the Year 7 English class where you were taught how to identify persuasive techniques. Think about things as much as possible.

Please just don't get the AI do it for you.

On a more positive note, here's some recent good things:

  • Got to see a tawny frogmouth up close recently - in the middle of the day! One has nested in a tree near the university's engineering precinct.
  • Finished my final assessment for the semester today! Officially only one semester to go! <3
  • Went and saw 'You Can See Everything' with Han last week and I can't stop talking and thinking about it. If you've seen it, please talk to me about it. If you haven't seen it, please go and see it!
  • Felt homesick the other day and made Mum's scalloped potatoes recipe! SO good.
  • The weather has been beautiful lately. Morning runs and walks have been extra fun. The other morning I ran past a guy walking barefoot through the park with a CAT in his backpack.
  • Made plans with Bec & Han to see 'Sunrise On The Reaping' next Monday - no spoilers if you've already seen it! Keen to talk about it after then.

Anyhow, happy almost-weekend!

-- Em

item.title: Jujutsu Primer (144 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ethanlowman.com/posts/jj-primer/, See on Hacker News

This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.

Why try Jujutsu?

jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git.

Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Installing jj

Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods:

# macOS
brew install jj

# Arch Linux
pacman -S jujutsu

# NixOS (ideally from nixpkgs-unstable)
nix-shell -p jujutsu

# From source
# (Requires a recent Rust and ~/.cargo/bin on your PATH)
cargo install --locked --bin jj jj-cli

Setup and configuration

In an existing git repository, run:

jj git init

From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:

jj config set --user user.name "Some One"
jj config set --user user.email "someone@example.com"

You can edit jj’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:

jj config edit --user

In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:

jj config list

Commits and changes

A commit, also called a revision, is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

When using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.

$ jj log
@  kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 849165bc
│  (empty) (no description set)
◆  royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d
│  Adjust config
~

The IDs on the left hand side (royxmykx and kpqxywon) are change IDs, which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon, we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k.

We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show, using its short prefix 2.

$ jj show 2
Commit ID: 2bea5e3d1992a60ba9ee52c6ce37c55adba9e8fb
Change ID: royxmykxtrkrqppotnrvutxlvrvqyxmy
Bookmarks: main main@git main@origin
Author   : Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:10:46)
Committer: Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:10:46)

    Adjust config

diff --git a/config.py b/config.py
index 7366a4e31d..174ffea06b 100644
--- a/config.py
+++ b/config.py
@@ -1,1 +1,1 @@
-DEFAULT_LIMIT = 10
+DEFAULT_LIMIT = 20

Many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta. See configuration docs if you’re interested.

Creating & evolving changes

Let’s take another look at our commit graph:

$ jj log
@  kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 849165bc
│  (empty) (no description set)
◆  royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d
│  Adjust config
~

On commit 849165bc, you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy, or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:

jj show shows commit details and a diff, which is empty here. 

$ jj show
Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a
Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk
Author   : Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:17:12)
Committer: Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:17:12)

    (no description set)

jj status shows repo state with diff stats. 

$ jj status
The working copy has no changes.
Working copy  (@) : kpqxywon 849165bc (empty) (no description set)

When we run a jj command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, jj automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change.

Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later).

Revsets

A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most jj commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran jj new k, the argument k was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID kpqxywon. The jj log command has an -r <REVSET> flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow.

Parent of @:

$ jj log -r @-
○  kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2
│  Implement the feature
~

Grandchildren of r:

$ jj log -r r++
@  qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a
│  Document the feature
~

○  nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e1b06678
│  Use the feature
~

Commits between r and @, inclusive:

$ jj log -r r::@
@  qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a
│  Document the feature
○  kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2
│  Implement the feature
◆  royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d
│  Adjust config
~

Commit k and all descendants:

$ jj log -r k::
@  qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a
│  Document the feature
│ ○  nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e1b06678
├─┘  Use the feature
○  kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2
│  Implement the feature
~

Commits authored by ethan@example.com that also have ID k or q:

$ jj log -r 'author("ethan@example.com") & (k | q)'
@  qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a
│  Document the feature
○  kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2
│  Implement the feature
~

I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced jj documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible.

For example, if we edit my_new_feature’s implementation in main.py and then run jj log, we’ll see that changes k, n, and q all get new commit IDs. jj also tells us that it performed a rebase.

Handling conflicts

If the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, jj doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like git rebase would. Instead, jj records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. Squash workflow

Editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your new changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation.

Let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a new commit on top of the conflicted commit:

Bookmarks and Git branches

jj does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks.

You can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. jj explicitly models bookmarks this way. jj bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote.

We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the jj docs on Working with GitHub.

Pushing a new branch

Assuming we initialized jj in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for jj git remote list.

$ jj git remote list
origin git@github.com:ethanal/example.git

Since jj is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, jj doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change).

To create a generated bookmark for change ID nlrtlrxv and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following:

Since jj git push -c creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR.

Updating a branch

To update a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create new commits and move the bookmark forward.

Bookmark squash flow

If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows.

First, create a new commit on top of our branch. 

$ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk
Working copy  (@) now at: stzvpxow f14a0cf7 (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature
Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files

Then make our edits. 

$ jj status
Working copy changes:
M README.md
Working copy  (@) : stzvpxow 6bdd43dc (no description set)
Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature

Squash them into the bookmark branch. 

$ jj squash --from @ --into push-nlrtlrxvuusk
Working copy  (@) now at: xryuuprx 04d65a03 (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Use the feature

We now see push-nlrtlrxvuusk has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them. 

$ jj git push -b push-nlrtlrxvuusk
Changes to push to origin:
  bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b]

The remote branch now reflects the new changes. The above output says that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. jj git push runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease, so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the jj git push --dry-run flag. jj protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads.

Bookmark advance flow

In this flow, we add new commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit.

Let’s first prepare the new commit. 

$ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk
Working copy  (@) now at: pptrztmx 6e49ff1f (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature

Then make our edits.

$ jj status
Working copy changes:
M README.md
Working copy  (@) : pptrztmx 89027165 (no description set)
Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature

$ jj commit -m "Add a usage example"
Working copy  (@) now at: wunttkrp 044f2d98 (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : pptrztmx 2341ee4a Add a usage example

The bookmark does not automatically move to our new commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now push-nlrtlrxvuusk still points at the commit below:

$ jj log -r n::
@  wunttkrp ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:51:57 044f2d98
│  (empty) (no description set)
○  pptrztmx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:51:57 2341ee4a
│  Add a usage example
○  nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:43:16 push-nlrtlrxvuusk aeb869ae
│  Use the feature
~

There are several ways to move the bookmark to the new commit. The easiest is probably jj bookmark advance, which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit:

$ jj bookmark advance --to @-
Advanced 1 bookmarks to pptrztmx 2341ee4a push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Add a usage example

Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark.

$ jj git push -b push-nlrtlrxvuusk
Changes to push to origin:
  bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move forward from aeb869aef99b to 2341ee4aa554]

Checking out a remote branch

Since jj is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a git fetch, importing remote bookmarks:

$ jj git fetch

And create a new empty commit on top of the remote branch:

$ jj new some-cool-feature@origin

Our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to git, we see that from git’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch.

$ git status
Not currently on any branch.
nothing to commit, working tree clean

This is because jj is editing a commit above a bookmark, and does not have an equivalent to git’s “current branch” state.

Pulling in changes from the trunk

Syncing with the trunk (e.g. main) is just a specific example of this flow. We would jj git fetch to update our main to the upstream main, and then rebase our commits on top. For example, the following would rebase my-branch on top of a new main:

jj rebase -b my-branch -o main

Staying oriented in the graph

jj commit graph manipulation is easiest when you have a live commit graph on screen. There are different ways you can accomplish this.

jjui is a TUI for jj that allows you to edit the visual graph directly. I have not personally used this, but I know people who like it.

I prefer to have an always-live jj log in the corner of my screen by way of viddy (a nicer version of watch that supports color):

viddy -t -n1 jj log --ignore-working-copy --color=always

I recommend filtering down this log to a revset that represents your current work. Here’s a starting point:

visible() & (trunk() | (tracked_remote_bookmarks() & ~::trunk()) | (mutable() & mine())::)

You might also consider trying my experimental project jj-stamp, which is a local code review GUI for the squash workflow. Even if you don’t use the squash review workflow, it makes a pretty good diff viewer with a live jj log on the side and a terminal for running jj operations.

Stacked PRs, in brief

One of the biggest productivity gains from jj comes in its ability to support stacked PR workflows. This merits its own post, so I’ll keep it short.

Large changes are easier to understand when they’re broken up into a series of logical steps. Breaking up a large change into smaller sequential atoms of review makes the whole change easier to understand. Stacked PRs attempt to leverage this fact to optimize merge throughput, while simultaneously removing pipeline stalls in the review process.

Let’s say we’re building a new feature. We can decide we want to split up implementation into three stages:

  1. Refactor to make the feature easier to implement
  2. Implement the feature
  3. Use the feature in another system

jj’s ability to work on stacked changes with automatic rebase is a natural fit for implementing these three stages. Each of the three stages maps to a single commit, each with an associated bookmark/branch/PR:

$ jj log -r oomyzqmz::sxummoow
○  sxummoow ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 14:10:48 ethan/sxummoow b5f0af21
│  Use the feature
○  vqpzktsp ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 14:06:27 ethan/vqpzktsp fe52c25f
│  Implement the feature
○  oomyzqmz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 14:01:19 ethan/oomyzqmz 07f69717
│  Refactor for the feature
~

After you implement the first change, you can put up a PR for review and immediately start working on the next change. Your work stream becomes a long queue where you pop off the bottom as PRs are ready to merge and push to the top, with no pipeline stalls.

It’s pretty easy to manually set up small PR stacks with jj and GitHub, but once you get hooked on the technique (making stacks 5–10 PRs deep), you’ll want a tool. jj-pancake is my entry into the ring of stacked PR tools. More on that soon.

Resources

  • Official Jujutsu docs. I most often refer to the revset spec.
  • Steve Klabnik’s jj tutorial was my first introduction to jj. I don’t think it’s maintained as a durable resource (and I don’t promise mine will be!), but it’s still a good read.
  • I follow the jj releases RSS feed. Lately the releases have been packed with new features. Overall jj is quite stable, but the occasional bug is fixed promptly.
  • The Jujutsu discord is active and friendly!
  • The blog of East River Source Control, a company that is building a new forge and code review platform intended to support Jujutsu well. The creator of Jujutsu, Martin von Zweigbergk, has joined as the CTO, and they have lots of other smart people as well. Perhaps a successor to GitHub one day? I’m rooting for them.
  • My personal jj config. You might find some useful aliases or tricks here, but I haven’t attempted to make it readable.
  • The jj config of Austin Seipp, a jj maintainer. Cool tricks lie within.

Get packages & executable files

Get the Sources

You can retrieve the source code through Git by using the command: 

git clone https://git.ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg.git ffmpeg

Cannot access Git or wish to speed up the cloning and reduce the bandwidth usage?

FFmpeg has always been a very experimental and developer-driven project. It is a key component in many multimedia projects and has new features added constantly. Development branch snapshots work really well 99% of the time so people are not afraid to use them.

Git Repositories

Since FFmpeg is developed with Git, multiple repositories from developers and groups of developers are available.

Release Verification

All FFmpeg releases are cryptographically signed with our public PGP key and should be verified for authenticity. 

pub   rsa2048 2011-04-26 [SC]
    FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8
uid           [  full  ] FFmpeg release signing key <ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org>
sub   rsa2048 2011-04-26 [E]

To verify a release:

  1. Import our public key into your local keyring: 
    $ curl https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-devel.asc | gpg --import
  2. Download a release tarball and its corresponding signature.
  3. Verify the signature: 
    $ gpg --verify ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz.asc ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz
gpg: Signature made Sun 21 Feb 2021 06:35:15 AEST
gpg:                using RSA key FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8
gpg:                issuer "ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org"
gpg: Good signature from "FFmpeg release signing key <ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org>" [full]

Optionally, you can verify that git and tarball match, the only differences should be the absence of .git* files in the tarball and a VERSION file in the tarball containing the version. The git tags should be signed with EDDSA key DD1EC9E8DE085C629B3E1846B18E8928B3948D64

A release that also has a .pq.asc file carries post-quantum signatures (RFC 9980) made with both of these keys: 

ML-DSA-87+Ed448  99669C49693683D51F174FE0D9E84915F5C2A536F5C0DA70FB8DCBD8AA8C4B3D
SLH-DSA-256s     547721479F80449E77748C0235116A1F8A73D9ECA98673B90E4E39347D229989

GnuPG cannot verify these yet; use sq 1.4 or later built with a cryptographic backend that supports these algorithms (OpenSSL 3.5 or RustCrypto), both of these must succeed: 

$ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-mldsa87-ed448.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz
$ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-slhdsa256s.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz

Approximately every 6 months the FFmpeg project makes a new major release. Between major releases point releases will appear that add important bug fixes but no new features. item.title: GIMP now has UI tests (126 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.gimp.org/news/2026/11/16/gimp-ui-tests/, See on Hacker News

GIMP has a lot of intertwined menus, dialogs and tools. When we change a part of the interface, another may stop working and sometimes, the problem can be missed until a user reports it.

To find these problems early, a new GUI testing platform was implemented. A typical GUI test starts GIMP, clicks menus and buttons, and then checks the result. These tests run automatically each time we merge contributor changes.

Why we need them⁠

GIMP already has unit tests. A unit test checks one small part of the code, for example how GIMP reads an XCF file. But our unit tests were not opening a real window. So it coult not tell us if a dialog opens, or if a menu item did its job.

Note that GIMP already had tests of GUI code, usually interacting directly with the core code, and sometimes even simulating input devices’ events (pointer movements, clicks, drags…). But nothing can beat interacting with the real interface. Furthermore such legacy tests directly hijacking core code come with their own problems, such as breaking all too often (and not because they detected a bug), all while not being able to detect whole categories of bugs.

UI tests check the program as a whole, in the same way as you use it.

What the tests do⁠

Each test starts a real GIMP and does one small task. Then it reads the result from GIMP. If the result is not correct, the test fails and tells us what went wrong.

We have 13 tests at this time. They check that:

  • GIMP starts and shows its main window.
  • The Welcome dialog opens on the correct tab. It also stays hidden when you turn off “Show on Start”.
  • File > New makes an image with the size you set.
  • File > Export As writes a correct PNG file.
  • Tools > Swap Colors swaps the foreground and background colors.
  • You can type a new foreground color in the Colors dialog.
  • You can add a layer and delete a layer.
  • Undo and Redo work.
  • Zoom In changes the zoom level.
  • A click on a tool button in the toolbox selects that tool. The test then uses the Bucket Fill tool on the canvas.
  • A change in Preferences is saved when you click OK.
  • A menu action, Image > Flatten Image, does its job.

How they work⁠

The tests do not need a screen. Each test starts a small, hidden desktop, runs GIMP in it, and removes it at the end. Because of this, the tests can run on our CI servers, where no screen is available.

To find a button or a menu, the tests do not look at the pixels on the screen. They use the accessibility information that GIMP gives to tools such as screen readers. This has one more good result: when we make GIMP easier to test, we also make it easier to use with a screen reader, hence improve the software accessibility.

The tests use dogtail, a Python tool for UI tests. To run GIMP on a server with no screen, dogtail needed a new feature. We contributed this feature upstream, to dogtail itself, so other projects can use it too.

At this time, the tests run only on Linux (both X11 and Wayland) since dogtail does not support Windows or macOs.

Adding even these few simple tests considerably increases confidence that the GIMP build has worked, and also shows the test infrastructure is working and useful.

Credits⁠

  • Harsh Verma wrote the UI tests and the new dogtail feature.
  • Jehan reviewed the UI tests.
  • Michal Odehnal reviewed the new dogtail feature.

You can read the full change in merge request !2909.

How you can help⁠

13 tests is a good start, but GIMP has many more dialogs and tools. If you want to help, you can write a test for the part of GIMP that you use the most.

We wrote a guide that shows how to write a new test and how to find the cause when a test fails: UI tests on developer.gimp.org.

We hope this work will help us find bugs earlier and keep GIMP working well for everyone.

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 (246 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/19.0/, See on Hacker News

E.1. Release 19 #

Release date: 2026-11-19

E.1.1. Overview #

PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including:

  • New REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance. REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) allows repacking without blocking reads and writes to the table.

  • pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies plan advice automatically based on the query.

  • Better performance in many areas, including automatic scaling of the number of I/O worker processes, quicker foreign-key checks, and further planning and execution optimizations.

  • Logical replication can now be enabled without a server restart when wal_level is set to replica.

  • Logical replication of sequence values.

  • Support for “read-your-writes” consistency on standbys via the new WAIT command.

  • Parallel autovacuum of table indexes and autovacuum prioritization through a new scoring system.

The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 19 are explained in more detail in the sections below.

E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 #

A dump/restore using pg_dumpall or use of pg_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. See Section 18.6 for general information on migrating to new major releases.

Version 19 contains a number of changes that may affect compatibility with previous releases. Observe the following incompatibilities:

  • Add server variable password_expiration_warning_threshold to warn about password expiration (Gilles Darold, Nathan Bossart) §

    The default warning period is seven days.

  • Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) §

    The warning can be disabled via server variable md5_password_warnings. MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in PostgreSQL 18.

  • Remove RADIUS support (Thomas Munro) §

    PostgreSQL only supported RADIUS over UDP, which is unfixably insecure.

  • Force standard_conforming_strings to always be on in the database server (Tom Lane) §

    Dumps created using pre-PostgreSQL 19 versions of pg_dump or pg_dumpall, and using standard_conforming_strings = off, will not properly load into PostgreSQL 19 and later servers. Users should create dumps using PostgreSQL 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on.

    Client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off, for compatibility with old servers. The server variable escape_string_warning has been removed as unnecessary.

  • Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) §

    pg_upgrade will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems.

  • Change the default index opclasses for inet and cidr data types from btree_gist to GiST (Tom Lane) § §

    The btree_gist inet/cidr opclasses are broken because they can exclude rows that should be returned. pg_upgrade will disallow upgrading of clusters with btree_gist inet/cidr indexes.

  • Disallow system columns from being used in COPY FROM ... WHERE (Tom Lane) §

    The values of such columns were not well-defined.

  • Change a json_array() call which returns no rows to return an empty JSON array (Richard Guo) §

    This previously returned NULL.

  • Cause transactions to pass their READ ONLY and DEFERRABLE status to postgres_fdw sessions (Etsuro Fujita) §

    This means READ ONLY transactions can no longer modify rows processed by postgres_fdw sessions.

  • Change default of max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128 (Heikki Linnakangas) §

    Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases.

  • Remove server variable io_workers (Thomas Munro) §

    This has been replaced by four new variables; see Section E.1.3.1.2.

  • Change JIT to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) §

    Previously JIT was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable JIT.

  • Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) §

    Previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by vacuum_cost_limit. With this change, VACUUM with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases.

  • Rename column sync_error_count to sync_table_error_count in system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Vignesh C) §

    This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately.

  • Rename wait event type BUFFERPIN to BUFFER and rename wait event BufferPin to BufferCleanup (Andres Freund) §

  • Remove wait event BufferContent and add more precise wait events BufferShared, BufferShareExclusive, and BufferExclusive (Andres Freund) §

  • Change index access method handlers to use a static IndexAmRoutines structure, rather than dynamically allocated ones (Matthias van de Meent) §

  • Remove optimizer hook get_relation_info_hook and add better-placed hook build_simple_rel_hook (Robert Haas) §

  • Change psql's \crosstabview command to honor the \pset null setting (Chao Li) §

  • Change full text search and pg_trgm to use the database's locale provider for character classification when parsing text (Jeff Davis) §

    Previously, characters were classified using libc, regardless of the locale provider. In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., ICU, builtin) and where the locale configured through that locale provider behaves differently from the LC_CTYPE setting configured for the database, particularly a LC_CTYPE of C, the output of some full text search and pg_trgm functions could change. When upgrading such databases using pg_upgrade, it is recommended to reindex all indexes which use full text search and pg_trgm after the upgrade, and to recompute any stored tsvector values.

  • Change how fuzzystrmatch functions handle non-ASCII characters (Peter Eisentraut, Jeff Davis) § §

    dmetaphone() and dmetaphone_alt() now upper-case their input using the database's default collation rather than always using libc, and soundex(), metaphone(), and difference() now treat only ASCII letters as letters. When upgrading with pg_upgrade, it is recommended to reindex any indexes that use these functions after the upgrade.

  • Remove MULE_INTERNAL encoding (Thomas Munro) §

    This encoding was complex and rarely used. Databases using it will need to be dumped and restored with a different encoding.

E.1.3. Changes #

Below you will find a detailed account of the changes between PostgreSQL 19 and the previous major release.

E.1.3.1. Server #

E.1.3.1.1. Optimizer #

  • Allow NOT IN clauses to be converted to more efficient ANTI JOINs when NULLs are not present (Richard Guo) §

  • Allow more LEFT JOINs to be converted to ANTI JOINs (Tender Wang, Richard Guo) §

  • Allow use of Memoize for ANTI JOINs with unique inner sides (Richard Guo) §

  • Allow some aggregate processing to be performed before joins (Richard Guo, Antonin Houska) § § §

    This can reduce the number of rows needed to be processed.

  • Improve hash join's handling of tuples with NULL join keys (Tom Lane) §

  • Improve the planning of semijoins (Richard Guo) §

  • Allow Append and MergeAppend to consider explicit incremental sorts (Richard Guo) §

  • Convert IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM NULL to IS [NOT] NULL during constant folding (Richard Guo) §

    The latter form is more easily optimized.

  • Simplify IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM to equality/inequality operators when inputs are proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) §

  • Perform earlier constant folding of var IS [NOT] NULL in the optimizer (Richard Guo) §

    This allows for later optimizations.

  • Simplify COALESCE() and ROW(...) IS [NOT] NULL to avoid evaluating unnecessary arguments (Richard Guo) § §

item.title: Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented (120 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://seremot.com/p/vint-cerf-on-why-tcpip-was-never, See on Hacker News

EXTRA, extra! Today I’m launching Future Stories, my own podcast about technology, science and the way we live.

The first guest is Vint Cerf. He co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn in the 1970s, the rules that let the world’s networks talk to each other. Interviewing him was on my bucket list for years. When I was at Cloudflare I thought about asking him many times, but I was a bit shy. He’s Vint Cerf, after all. This year I finally asked, and he said yes.

We talked over Zoom (not using Zoom again) on October 14. He’s 83, he left Google this year after more than twenty years, and he’s helping start a company, Tolero, that is building software for an Internet between planets. His words: “the speed of light is too slow.”

“Who will our allies be 25 years from now? And we didn’t know. So we thought the only way we can be assured that the allies will have access to this is to simply open it up.”

First, a bug related one (ring a bell? those never stopped over the years…). Vint once spent two weeks on a program that failed at random, so he couldn’t reproduce it. He finally asked his best friend, Steve Crocker, to step through it with him. At one point Crocker said “that’s the problem”, and he was right. Thirty seconds, after two weeks. Vint’s takeaway is that this is why collaboration matters.

Then a bottle of glitter. In late 1989 three commercial Internet services started in the United States, and one of them was called CERFnet, in San Diego. They first wanted to call it SURFnet, because surfing the Internet, but a network in the Netherlands had a name too close to it. So they asked Vint if they could use his.

He had a moment of “what if they screw it up?”, then decided that people name kids after other people and nobody blames the person they were named after. At the launch, he and the network’s director smashed a plastic bottle of glitter over a Cisco router.

He also tried to connect Minitel, the French online service, to MCI Mail, the email service he built in the 1980s. MCI Mail was designed to link to everything. It reached the telegraph system, which he calls 19th-century stuff, and fax. It even reached the post office: type a postal address into the email and they printed it, put it in an envelope and mailed it. Minitel refused to connect, and he says he still doesn’t understand why.

One more, from outside the interview: In 2020, someone on the Internet-history mailing list (I’m on it) asked if anyone had ever seen Vint without a three-piece suit. One reply: “I have seen Vint in a t-shirt!” Vint answered with just a photo, “IP on Everything”, from a 1992 engineers’ meeting where, in his words, he “felt compelled” to do an “IP on Everything” striptease. The thread is public.

We didn’t go very deep into AI. Time was short, and it’s not his main field these days. But even there, he has a clear way of thinking about it. And near the end he shows a piece of the original ARPANET on camera, and talks about his worry that the next century won’t be able to read what we leave behind.

“I’m worried that the 22nd century won’t know what happened in the 21st because all of our records will have evaporated or will be uninterpretable.”

The full conversation is 56 minutes, with chapters:

You can also read the transcript at ourfuturestories.eu/vint-cerf, or listen in your favourite podcast app: ourfuturestories.eu/subscribe. A Portuguese article about it is on SAPO. Short clips are coming in the next days.

This is a passion project. The idea is to tell good stories, the kind that hold up over time. If you like it, subscribe, share it with a friend, and tell me who I should talk to next, you can do it here: ourfuturestories.eu/#contact.

Stay tuned, geek out!

———

Fun fact: in 2024 I did a segment on the 50 years of the TCP paper on my previous podcast, This Week in NET at Cloudflare. My guests were three then-colleagues: Mark Nottingham (standards), Marwan Fayed (research) and Lucas Pardue (web protocols, co-chair of the IETF’s QUIC working group). You can listen here (or below).

The paper is “A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication”, by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, published in May 1974 in IEEE Transactions on Communications. It described TCP, a way to join many packet networks into a network of networks. TCP was later split into TCP and IP, and in 1983 they became the core of the Internet that DARPA launched.

ChatGPT for SNES

ChatGPT for SNES can make mistakes.

Type on your keyboard. Enter sends. Backspace deletes; Page Up and Page Down scroll. It simulates a control pad entry.Your keys are the controller: arrows, X = A, Z = B, A = Y, Enter = Start.

Your keys are the controller: arrows, X = A, Z = B, A = Y, Enter = Start.

Letters move the cursor on the game's keyboard and type. Enter sends. The touch buttons work too (B deletes).

Download the v0.7 ROM (1.5 MB zip: one .sfc file). Requires a flash cart with Super FX support, such as an FXPak Pro or an sd2snes with current firmware. Leave Chip Options › SuperFX speed at Normal. The build with the fact book (17 MB zip: the .sfc and its .msu file) also needs MSU-1 support: put both files in the same folder with their names unchanged.

  • ChatGPT for SNES is an unofficial experiment designed by Benj Edwards and coded by AI agents: a ChatGPT-style chat program for the Super Nintendo. Its training conversations were written by gpt-oss-120b, OpenAI's open-weight model. Not made or endorsed by OpenAI.
  • This is version 0.7 (2 November 2026).
  • A small language model with about 2.2 million parameters runs on the cartridge's Super FX 2 chip and writes its answers one word at a time.
  • In the main build every word it writes comes from the language model. A second build adds a fact book (the opening sentences of 150,000 Simple English Wikipedia articles, stored in the cartridge's MSU-1 data file): like ChatGPT searching the web, its model can decide to look something up and print what the book says.
  • Here it runs in the Snes9x emulator in your browser; the first visit loads about 4 MB (19 MB with the fact book).
  • Press Start (Enter) on the title screen, then type on your keyboard and press Enter to send. Each letter takes a moment to appear, because the page moves the cursor on the game's own on-screen keyboard.
  • It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently. The fact book can carry mistakes too.

On a real Super NES

If you liked this, you might enjoy Séance, which runs a tiny AI language model on a real NES.

  • Responses and context: the openai plugin

  • The full configuration
  • What changed on the code side
  • Caveats

I wrote an article a couple of months ago describing how I rebuilt my old voice assistant pipeline in Platypush.

And I wrote earlier articles describing my journey through self-hosted voice assistants - in 2024 (with Picovoice), in 2020 (diving into the legacy assistant.google integration, the now defunct assistant.alexa integration, the now defunct Snowboy integration, the now defunct DeepSpeech integration and Picovoice) and the original article in 2019 describing the Google Assistant integration.

For a couple of months I used the voice pipeline described in my latest article as my main driver, but after getting used to the robustness of commercial voice assistants I was unhappy with the high rates of false positives/negatives of my self-hosted pipeline, as well as its lack of robustness in detecting start/end of speech, especially in noisy environments and using cheap microphones.

After a bit of experimentation, I decided to swap and fine tune a few parts, and after a couple of days of trying the results are satisfying enough for me to write a short article about it.

The resulting pipeline is:

Wake word detection: a new assistant.microwakeword plugin

Until recently I used assistant.openwakeword, which wraps openWakeWord.

It works, but the project has been quiet for a while and all of its pre-trained models are v0.1 files from 2023, mostly trained on synthetic speech.

In practice I was getting both false positives (the hotword triggering on background noise) and false negatives (the hotword not detected unless I was close to the microphone).

I added a new plugin, assistant.microwakeword, on top of microWakeWord through the pymicro-wakeword Python bindings.

microWakeWord is the engine used by ESPHome and Home Assistant Voice, its models are actively maintained, and the built-in models (okay_nabu, hey_jarvis, hey_mycroft, alexa) ship with the package — no download required.

The current official models are provided under the ESPHome micro-wake-word-models repository.

Custom models are supported too: drop a microWakeWord JSON manifest (with its .tflite model) in the plugin's models directory and reference it by name.

The plugin exposes the same API as assistant.openwakeword (same models, detection_threshold, frame_duration, patience_frames, input_device, input_volume parameters, same list_models action, same HotwordDetectedEvent), so switching is a matter of just changing the configuration to point to the new plugin:

assistant.microwakeword:
  models:
    - alexa

A few design notes:

  • Without an explicit detection_threshold, each model uses the probability_cutoff from its own manifest (0.9 for alexa), which is the value the model was validated against.
  • Models already smooth their output over a sliding window, so unlike openwakeword, patience_frames defaults to 0 here.
  • The audio thread never touches the TFLite models directly: it queues frames (and a reset marker) to the main thread, because MicroWakeWord.reset() reloads the interpreter and isn't safe to call concurrently.
  • Like assistant.openwakeword, the plugin releases the audio device when another assistant plugin starts a conversation, and re-acquires it when the conversation ends.

Speech-to-text: assistant.openai, with a much better ear

assistant.openai records audio when a conversation starts and transcribes it through Whisper.

The tricky part has always been end-of-speech detection: knowing when the user has finished talking. The previous implementation used a per-frame boolean from WebRTC VAD, and any single frame classified as speech would reset the silence timer. With even a bit of background noise, phrases would only end when the maximum conversation duration was hit.

The audio preprocessing layer (AudioPreprocessor, shared by the STT integrations) has been reworked:

  • Silero VAD as the primary backend (through onnxruntime, no PyTorch required), with WebRTC VAD and a plain RMS-based detector as fallbacks. To get an idea of Silero VAD's performance compared against other solutions for speech activity detection, take a look at the insightful article One voice detector to rule them all. The Silero model is downloaded on first use into the Platypush workdir and checksum-verified:
assistant.openai:
  # auto = silero -> webrtc -> energy, depending on what's installed
  vad_backend: auto

  • Hysteresis + sliding window: a frame becomes speech above the VAD threshold and stays speech until its score drops by a margin, and the per-frame decisions are smoothed by majority vote over a 0.5s window. A single noise burst can no longer keep a conversation alive.

  • Adaptive noise floor: the background noise level is tracked over time, and frames that aren't louder than noise_floor_factor (default 2.0, ~6 dB) times the floor are never considered as speech.

On a synthetic benchmark (Piper-generated phrases mixed with babble and burst noise), the old settings kept conversations open for 6–10 seconds after the speech had ended; the new pipeline ends them 1.0–1.6 seconds after the last word, which is the configured conversation_end_timeout plus the smoothing lag.

Since the changes on Platypush have been performed directly in the AudioPreprocessor also used by other native speech-to-text engines, other speech-to-text plugins also benefit from them - e.g. if you use assistant.vosk for full on-device detection.

Responses and context: the openai plugin

The transcribed phrase is processed by the openai plugin, which handles both the API key and the conversation context. By default the assistant renders the response through the configured tts_plugin; if the response ends with a question mark, the conversation continues with a follow-up.

Custom hooks can intercept phrases before the default response kicks in — for example, to handle home automation commands locally without an LLM round-trip:

from platypush import run, when
from platypush.message.event.assistant import SpeechRecognizedEvent

@when(SpeechRecognizedEvent, phrase='play (the)? music')
def play_music():
    run('music.mpd.play')

And the hotword event is wired to the conversation start with a similar hook:

from platypush import run, when
from platypush.message.event.assistant import HotwordDetectedEvent

@when(HotwordDetectedEvent)
def on_hotword(**_):
    run('assistant.openai.start_conversation')

Text-to-speech: tts.openai

Responses are rendered by tts.openai, with volume and voice configurable. In my tests however tts.piper also yielded good results, and it runs entirely locally. In my tests on a RaspberryPi 5 however it added ~3-4s of latency to process the response to audio compared to tts.openai.

Since the TTS output goes to the speakers and the wake word detector listens on the microphone, the assistant plugins pause hotword detection while a conversation is active — otherwise the assistant would hear itself.

The full configuration

openai:
  api_key: YOUR_API_KEY
  # Or, for a custom setup using a model provider compatible with the OpenAI API,
  # e.g. a local Ollama instance:
  # base_url: http://localhost:8000/v1
  # model: gpt-5
  # Optional context that can be passed to initialize the assistant
  # context:
  #   role: system
  #   content: You are a useful assistant.

assistant.microwakeword:
  models:
    - alexa

assistant.openai:
  tts_plugin: tts.openai
  conversation_start_sound: ~/sounds/wake_word_detected.wav
  input_volume: 100

# assistant.vosk:
#   model: /path/to/vosk/model
#   conversation_start_sound: ~/sounds/wake_word_detected.wav
#   input_volume: 100

tts.openai:
  output_volume: 80.0

# Or, for a fully local setup that uses tts.piper:
# tts.piper:
#   output_volume: 80.0

What changed on the code side

  • New assistant.microwakeword plugin: microWakeWord hotword detection through pymicro-wakeword, same API as assistant.openwakeword, built-in models bundled with the package, custom models via JSON manifests.
  • assistant.openwakeword fixes: frames are now 80ms (1280 samples, the size openWakeWord recommends) instead of 500ms — longer chunks only return the highest score over their sub-frames and can miss hotwords — plus a patience_frames parameter (consecutive frames above threshold) and an explicit detection_threshold parameter (default 0.5).
  • Shared AudioPreprocessor rework: Silero/WebRTC/energy VAD backends with vad_backend: auto selection, threshold hysteresis, sliding-window majority vote, and an adaptive noise floor. Used by both assistant.openai and assistant.vosk.
  • New Silero VAD wrapper: ONNX inference through onnxruntime, recurrent state carried across frames, checksum-verified model download into the workdir.

Caveats

The microphone on my RPi doesn't support 16 kHz natively, so audio is captured at 44.1 kHz and software-resampled — it works, but if detection feels sluggish software resampling is usually the first suspect.

The VAD and threshold defaults were tuned on synthetic audio plus a couple of my audio recordings.

Different rooms, microphones and acoustics may yield different results. You may want to adjust detection_threshold on the wake word plugin and noise_floor_factor on the STT plugins if you don't feel satisfied with your mileage.
